ECE 6612

TLS records, downgrade paths and limits

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a network attacker encountering certificate checks, authenticated records and an application’s HTTPS upgrade policy at different stages.

A browser request crosses routing, DNS and transport machinery before reaching its TLS peer. Poisoning DNS or redirecting packets can move the connection toward an attacker-controlled host. Certificate-name validation and handshake authentication still require proof for the intended site. An attacker with no acceptable credential can cause a failed connection or relay encrypted traffic, rather than automatically becoming the authenticated endpoint.

After a successful modern TLS handshake, record authentication detects changed or fabricated application ciphertext, and encryption protects the payload from a passive network observer. Record sequence and nonce rules bind protection to protocol state. Packet addresses, timing and approximate encrypted lengths remain observable at the network boundary. A peer endpoint, trusted interception proxy or compromised application sees plaintext at its own termination point.

TLS version and cipher suite specify the actual record mechanisms. TLS 1.3 uses AEAD suites and removes many legacy options. TLS 1.2 supports AEAD and also older constructions. TLS 1.1 is deprecated and predates those modern requirements; evaluating an alleged attack requires the negotiated suite, implementation and required attacker capability. Merely stating an older version supplies no universal decryption procedure.

A network attacker may drop handshake messages to provoke an application’s legacy retry behavior. Changing version fields within an authenticated handshake changes its transcript and should fail the required checks. TLS 1.3 includes downgrade-detection values in ServerHello.random when a capable server negotiates an older version, allowing capable clients to detect certain forced downgrades. Actual downgrade outcomes depend on both endpoints’ support and fallback policy.

HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) tells a browser to require HTTPS for a host for a stated time, with optional subdomain coverage. A previously learned policy or preloaded entry protects the initial HTTP choice. On a first visit without such a policy, an attacker may interfere with an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect and keep the user on HTTP if the application permits it. This is a change in whether TLS is used at all, with different assumptions from negotiating a TLS version.

Certificate revocation addresses credentials that should no longer be accepted before their expiry. Signed revocation evidence can be checked for authenticity even when transported over an untrusted channel, while freshness and availability still matter. TLS also relies on protected endpoints and correct user/application decisions about certificate errors. A network attacker can continue to drop packets or disrupt TCP even when record cryptography remains sound.

A certificate revocation list (CRL) is a signed list that clients can download and cache; its update times determine freshness. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) answers status queries for individual certificates. OCSP stapling lets the server deliver a signed status response during the connection, reducing a client’s direct query to the status service. A client that continues when status checking is unavailable makes a different availability/security tradeoff from one that rejects the connection. Pinning restricts accepted keys or certificates further, while requiring a safe rollover and recovery plan.

Example

Assume a client requires TLS 1.2 or newer, validates shop.example correctly and has no compromised keys or implementation flaws. An attacker can drop packets and present a TLS 1.1-only endpoint. The required minimum prevents that session from completing. If a different client explicitly permits legacy fallback, analyze the newly negotiated suite and its specific weaknesses before claiming any plaintext recovery.

Practice

1. A client previously used TLS 1.2 and is now induced to connect using TLS 1.1. Is that information enough to conclude the attacker can read arbitrary application data? State the missing inputs needed for a defensible analysis.

Identify the concrete record protection and the attacker’s access to keys, oracles and endpoints.

The version change establishes use of a deprecated protocol, while arbitrary plaintext recovery requires a further capability or flaw. Determine the negotiated cipher suite, key exchange, certificate/identity validation, exact fallback path, implementation behavior and the attacker’s position and available oracles. Those inputs define which attacks apply.

2. A visitor has a valid saved HSTS policy for shop.example. An attacker poisons DNS to send the visitor to an unrelated server with a valid certificate only for thief.example. Which checks constrain the attack, and which service effect can the attacker still cause?

Evaluate HTTPS selection first and server-name authentication second.

HSTS requires HTTPS, and server-name validation rejects the unrelated certificate for shop.example. The attacker can still deny access by redirecting or dropping traffic. An accepted impersonating HTTPS endpoint would require an additional credential or validation compromise.
